subtitle: When someone reports discrimination or harassment, you will know how to respond appropriately at first, report immediately, handle information carefully and follow through accountably. The course gives you practice with each step.
scope: For leaders and supervisors responding to possible harassment or discrimination across DHS work settings. Follow current agency complaint, investigation, emergency, records, and employment procedures. This course does not investigate reports, judge credibility, establish violations, decide discipline, or replace internal or external reporting rights. Managers with assigned investigation or corrective-action duties must perform those duties under agency procedures and within their authorized role. Use practice material in learning activities rather than real complaint details.
introTranscript: A leader’s first response can determine whether a harassment or discrimination concern reaches the right process promptly. Minnesota Policies 1436 and 1329 require managers and supervisors to treat reports seriously, respond appropriately, and immediately report allegations or incidents to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer. This course follows practice reports involving an employee, a contractor, and an assignment change after reporting. Leaders practice listening without dismissing, preserving the reported facts without conducting an investigation outside assigned agency procedures or authority, coordinating the correct route, and preventing avoidable exposure or retaliatory treatment. Acknowledgment and immediate reporting do not decide the outcome; they make fair review possible.

intro.heading: Receive the report without making the employee prove it first
intro.body:
A person may report a concern hesitantly, without knowing which policy applies or having every detail ready. A manager should listen, acknowledge the account, and explain the next appropriate step. The report is not a finding, but incomplete information is not a reason to ignore it or require the person to investigate alone.

In a team in this example, an employee says that a colleague repeatedly mocks the employee’s accent and has linked that criticism to assignments. The manager should not respond that the employee is too sensitive, that the colleague is well liked, or that the concern will be accepted only after the employee proves intent. The reported conduct and work context can be accurately communicated to the person or area responsible.

Ask initial questions needed to understand and route the concern, using agency guidance. Avoid probing credibility through confrontation, gathering a personal case file, or inviting team debate. If an immediate-help concern is present, use the established urgent process as well. A respectful acknowledgment makes the next step clear without promising a particular outcome.

What should the manager do?
lessons.keyStatement: The first response opens the proper process; it does not decide the case.

flashcards.back: Information about possible harassment, discrimination, or retaliation, received directly or through awareness of a problem. It is not a finding.
A report that conduct or an employment decision relates to an actual or perceived characteristic protected by the applicable policy.
Information about possible unwelcome conduct or communication of a sexual nature, addressed through the separate applicable policy.
A manager’s duty to report allegations or incidents to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer without waiting to prove the case independently.
Preserving relevant facts through the approved complaint process and limiting unnecessary access or disclosure.
Possible prohibited treatment connected to opposing, reporting, or participating in the relevant process; coordinate review rather than deciding it alone.

items.title: Acknowledge
items.body: Explain that the concern has been heard and that the required route will be used. In the accent-related case, the employee needs a serious response, not assurance that the colleague probably meant well. Acknowledgment can remain neutral about findings while still being clear that reporting will occur.

items.title: Initial facts
items.body: Preserve the reported conduct, context, and relevant available details for appropriate routing. If the employee is unsure of a date, record that uncertainty rather than invent precision. The purpose is to get the account to the responsible process, not to demand a completed investigation before it can be reported.

items.title: Avoid blame
items.body: Questions about why the employee did not object sooner or why the colleague is admired can shift attention away from the report. Reporting delay or reputation does not settle what happened. Ask about relevant facts in a professional way and leave credibility assessment to the authorized process.

tabs.label: Proof gate
tabs.body: Requiring complete proof may feel protective against error, but delays the manager’s required reporting step and makes the person perform an investigation alone. The proper review process can examine evidence. Receive and route the account without deciding its validity at the doorway.

tabs.label: Serious acknowledgment
tabs.body: A serious acknowledgment explains the next step while reserving findings for the authorized process. It gives the employee useful information without promising discipline. This supports fair review for everyone rather than minimizing the report or deciding it instantly.

tabs.label: Instant agreement
tabs.body: Declaring a violation immediately can feel supportive but substitutes the manager’s conclusion for review. Do not promise punishment from an initial account. Take the report seriously, communicate it accurately, and preserve the responsible process’s authority.

check.question: Which response appropriately receives the accent-related report?
check.correct: Acknowledge it, preserve the relevant reported facts, and use the required reporting route without demanding complete proof.
wrong: Demand proof of intent before accepting it.
Dismiss it because the colleague is respected.
Promise the colleague will be dismissed.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response supports proper review without a proof barrier or a promised finding.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Intent proof, reputation, and instant punishment each bypass the proper process in a different way. The manager’s initial duty is to take the report seriously and route it appropriately, not require the employee to establish a violation or announce one.

items.text: Explain that the concern was heard and identify the next step.
Avoid promising a finding or discipline.
The employee describes the remarks and assignment context.
An uncertain date is recorded as uncertain.
Demand that the employee prove motive before reporting.
Use the colleague’s popularity to reject the concern.

lessons.next: Next: Identify the immediate manager reporting duty under the relevant state policies.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: An employee reports repeated accent-related mocking. The manager wants the employee to prove intent before the concern can reach HR.
options: Require a complete independent case first.
Receive the account seriously and immediately use the proper reporting route.
Ask the team to decide whether the employee is too sensitive.
responses: The proof gate delays the required response.
The authorized process can evaluate the relevant information.
A team judgment is not appropriate complaint review.

lessons.transfer: Draft a neutral acknowledgment with no blame, proof gate, or promised finding.

move.control: You can make the first response serious, accurate, and process-focused.
move.failure: A report is blocked until the person proves an outcome independently.

Do not substitute a private inquiry for the agency process.

lessons.statement: Do not delay the required route while trying to solve the case yourself.

intro.heading: Report immediately instead of conducting a private investigation
intro.body:
Policies 1436 and 1329 require managers and supervisors to immediately report allegations or incidents to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer. The duty is not postponed until the manager believes a violation is likely. It also applies when a manager is otherwise aware that a relevant problem exists. Use current agency procedures for the actual reporting step.

In the practice team, the manager considers interviewing three coworkers privately before deciding whether the accent-related concern deserves reporting. That sequence reverses the responsibility: the allegation should reach the person or area responsible immediately, and any investigation must follow the agency’s procedures.

A person may ask for secrecy because of concern about consequences. Listen respectfully and explain the reporting duty and appropriate information handling. Do not promise to keep a report outside the required process, and do not announce it widely. Proper coordination can be prompt and bounded; the manager should confirm the responsible route rather than invent an informal investigation role.

Distinguish appropriate reporting from a private credibility inquiry.
Plan a response when a person asks the manager not to forward the report.
How should the supervisor respond?
lessons.keyStatement: Do not delay the required route while trying to solve the case yourself.

items.title: Immediate duty
items.body: The relevant policies name HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer as recipients of immediate manager reporting. In the practice case, report the allegation through that route rather than first deciding whether the colleague’s explanation is persuasive. A factual uncertainty should be communicated, not used as a reason to delay.

items.title: Authorized investigation
items.body: Investigation must follow agency procedures and the person or area responsible’s guidance. A manager should not collect witness statements independently simply to decide whether reporting is worthwhile. Such an inquiry can influence accounts, expose information, or create records outside the appropriate process before the required office is involved.

items.title: Privacy explanation
items.body: Explain that the information will be handled through appropriate channels and that you have a reporting responsibility. A secrecy request deserves care, but cannot cancel the duty. Tell the person the next step without promising that no one will learn anything or that a particular outcome will follow.

tabs.label: Wait and investigate
tabs.body: Waiting for a private inquiry may seem thorough, but substitutes the manager’s threshold for the policy’s reporting duty. It can also delay response while facts or accounts change. Report immediately and coordinate any permitted next steps through the responsible process.

tabs.label: Report and coordinate
tabs.body: Immediate reporting places the information with the proper authority promptly. The manager can then follow agency guidance and provide relevant work context. It preserves fair review without treating the allegation as a proven result.

tabs.label: Secret agreement
tabs.body: A secret agreement may reassure the person briefly, but conflicts with the reporting responsibility and can leave the concern unaddressed. Explain limits honestly and keep information sharing purposeful. Privacy protection is different from keeping the matter outside its required route.

check.question: What should happen before a manager’s independent credibility interviews?
check.correct: Immediately report the allegation to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and follow agency guidance.
wrong: Obtain permission from the reported colleague.
Promise not to report if the person asks for secrecy.
check.feedbackCorrect: The required reporting step does not depend on a private finding, the reported person’s permission, or a secrecy agreement.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Private interviews, permission gates, and secrecy promises each delay or bypass the required report. The manager can preserve uncertainties and handle information carefully without deciding the case first. Immediately use the policy’s route and follow the agency process.

items.text: Immediately report to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer.
Report a relevant problem of which the manager is otherwise aware.
Ask the person or area responsible about the next permitted step.
Explain reporting and privacy limits accurately.
Interview coworkers first to decide whether HR deserves the report.
Wait for the reported colleague to authorize forwarding.

lessons.next: Next: Recognize that the policies extend beyond employee-to-employee office interactions.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: The employee asks the supervisor to keep an allegation secret. The supervisor knows the policy requires immediate reporting.
options: Agree to keep it outside the process indefinitely.
Explain the duty and appropriate handling, then immediately report through the required route.
Tell the entire team for transparency.
responses: The agreement conflicts with the reporting responsibility.
This is honest about the duty and careful about information.
Immediate reporting does not mean unrestricted disclosure.

lessons.transfer: Locate the current HR or Affirmative Action reporting route and write an accurate explanation of the duty.

move.control: You can report promptly and explain the limits of your role.
move.failure: An informal promise or private investigation replaces immediate reporting.

lessons.summary: Recognize that the policies extend beyond employee-to-employee office interactions.
lessons.objective: Recognize that the policies extend beyond employee-to-employee office interactions.
objectives: Recognize that the policies extend beyond employee-to-employee office interactions.
Choose appropriate coordination for a report involving a third party.
Explain internal routes without implying they remove external reporting options.
takeaways: Third-party interactions can fall within the policy scope.
A setting outside the office is not automatically outside the workplace concern.
Internal procedures do not remove applicable external options.
lessons.statement: Do not narrow a report out of the process because of who or where.

image.caption: Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

intro.heading: Include contractors, public-service settings, and external routes
intro.body:
The state harassment and discrimination policies cover employees and relevant third parties with business interactions, including contractors, vendors, applicants, and customers. They address conduct in or affecting the workplace or public service environment. A manager should not dismiss an account simply because it involves a contractor or occurred during service delivery away from the office.

In a practice procurement meeting, a contractor directs discriminatory remarks toward a staff member. The manager still needs to use the appropriate reporting route. Any response involving the contractual relationship or corrective action must be coordinated through the responsible authorities; the manager should not independently promise termination or tell staff that nothing can be done.

The policies identify internal complaint routes and state that individuals may also choose external legal channels such as EEOC or MDHR. Explain those options accurately without promising outcomes or giving an unverified deadline. Do not require consultant approval, an internal finding, or permission from the reported party before a person can consider an external route.

Choose appropriate coordination for a report involving a third party.
Explain internal routes without implying they remove external reporting options.
What should the manager do?
lessons.keyStatement: Do not narrow a report out of the process because of who or where.

items.title: Third parties
items.body: The contractor’s employment status does not make the conduct irrelevant. Preserve the reported context and immediately use the proper manager route. The authorized process can consider the relationship and appropriate action; the supervisor should not assume that employee discipline rules supply every answer for a vendor.

items.title: Public service
items.body: A service-related interaction away from the office can still affect the workplace or public service environment. In a practice site visit, describe who was involved and how the interaction relates to the work. Do not use location as an automatic exclusion without appropriate guidance.

items.title: External options
items.body: Internal procedures are encouraged, but the policies preserve external reporting choices. A leader can identify accurate resources and refer detailed legal or deadline questions appropriately. Avoid stating that someone must exhaust an internal conversation or obtain the consultant’s approval before considering those channels.

tabs.label: Employee-only assumption
tabs.body: An employee-only assumption is simple to administer but contradicts the policies’ broader scope. It may leave staff exposed to a recurring contractor problem. Use the appropriate reporting route and let the responsible authorities address the relationship and possible response.

tabs.label: Coordinated third-party response
tabs.body: Coordination brings HR or Affirmative Action and other appropriate authorities into the response. It can support a lawful, proportionate action without improvised contract decisions. A manager can still describe the incident accurately and follow immediate reporting duties.

tabs.label: Internal-only message
tabs.body: Telling staff the internal process is their only choice overstates the leader’s authority and the policy. Explain the internal route clearly while preserving external options. Detailed legal questions should go to the appropriate resource rather than a confident but unverified answer.

check.question: What is appropriate for the contractor-related report?
check.correct: Immediately use the proper reporting route and coordinate any third-party action through responsible authorities.
wrong: Dismiss it because the contractor is not an employee.
Tell the employee that no external route can be considered.
check.feedbackCorrect: The broader scope requires appropriate reporting, while corrective and legal decisions remain properly authorized.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Third-party status does not exclude the concern. A termination promise jumps ahead of authorized action, and an internal-only rule removes options the policies preserve. Report the account and coordinate the applicable response without making those unsupported claims.

items.text: A contractor’s reported conduct affects a staff member at work.
A service interaction away from the office involves reported protected-class remarks.
HR advises about the reporting and review process.
The appropriate authority considers the contractual response.
Only employees can be involved in a policy concern.
External reporting requires consultant permission.

options: Use the location to reject the report.
Immediately report and coordinate the applicable third-party and public-service response.
Promise a specific contract outcome without review.
responses: Location does not automatically exclude the reported work interaction.
This preserves the required route and proper decision authority.
Contract action requires the appropriate process.

lessons.transfer: Identify the reporting route and appropriate coordination for a practice third-party concern.

move.control: You can recognize scope and avoid false reporting restrictions.
move.failure: Who or where is used as a shortcut to dismiss the account.

lessons.title: Preserve relevant facts without exposing the account
lessons.summary: Separate a reported fact, uncertainty, and personal interpretation in a sample note.
lessons.objective: Separate a reported fact, uncertainty, and personal interpretation in a sample note.
objectives: Separate a reported fact, uncertainty, and personal interpretation in a sample note.
Identify inappropriate use of complaint details in team learning or chat.

takeaways: Record the account and uncertainty accurately.
Do not turn complaint details into a teaching story.
Use approved channels and guidance for information handling.
lessons.statement: Useful records are accurate, bounded, and kept in the proper process.

image.caption: Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

intro.heading: Preserve relevant facts without exposing the account
intro.body:
An account is more useful when the reported facts, uncertainties, and the manager’s actions are distinguishable. Avoid adding a motive or diagnosis the person did not report. If a date is uncertain, say so. If the manager observed an incident directly, distinguish that observation from information received from someone else.

In the practice team, the employee describes an accent-related remark and identifies a coworker who may have heard it. The manager should preserve that information through the agency’s approved process. Posting the account in a team chat to ask whether the remark was discriminatory exposes the report and creates an informal public review.

Use the person or area responsible’s instructions for records, access, and communication. Do not delete potentially relevant information, create an unrestricted personal file, or promise that all information can remain permanently secret. Learning activities should use practice material. An app exercise, consultation request, or report export is not a replacement for the agency complaint system.

inThisLesson: Separate a reported fact, uncertainty, and personal interpretation in a sample note.
Identify inappropriate use of complaint details in team learning or chat.
Plan approved record handling and communication with the person or area responsible.
What is the appropriate response?
lessons.keyStatement: Useful records are accurate, bounded, and kept in the proper process.

items.title: Separate information
items.body: A note can identify who reported what, what remains uncertain, and what action the manager took. For example, distinguish “the employee reports a comment last week” from a conclusion about the colleague’s intent. Clear separation improves review without pretending the initial note establishes all facts.

items.title: Approved handling
items.body: Follow the agency’s instructions for preserving and transmitting relevant material. If a message may be relevant, ask the person or area responsible how to handle it rather than deleting it or forwarding it broadly. The goal is reliable review within the authorized process, not maximum circulation.

items.title: Learning boundary
items.body: Do not use actual complaint details in course responses, team demonstrations, or exported learning reports. Even removing a name may leave an account recognizable. Use a practice case to practice the response and keep the real concern in the agency route that applies, with the person or area responsible.

tabs.label: Private personal file
tabs.body: A personal file may seem convenient for the supervisor, but can separate records from the authorized process and access rules. Coordinate approved handling with the person or area responsible. Preserve relevant information without creating a new unrestricted repository of allegations.

tabs.label: Accurate approved record
tabs.body: An accurate record supports review because reported facts, uncertainties, and actions remain distinct. Approved handling also limits unnecessary exposure. It does not guarantee a finding; it provides usable information for the process responsible for reaching one.

tabs.label: Team debate
tabs.body: Team debate can feel transparent, but turns colleagues into informal judges and exposes the person’s account. It can also shape witness recollections. Discuss general conduct expectations separately and keep the actual report within its proper route.

check.question: Which note is appropriate?
check.correct: An accurate account distinguishing reported information, uncertainty, and the manager’s required action, handled through the approved process.
wrong: A diagnosis added by the supervisor.
A public chat asking the team to judge the account.
A rewritten date that looks more certain than the report.
check.feedbackCorrect: The record supports proper review without adding invented facts or inviting unnecessary exposure.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A medical label, public debate, or invented precision adds material the process cannot rely on. Keep reported information, uncertainties, and actions distinguishable. Use approved handling rather than making the initial account a public or personal investigation file.

items.text: The employee reports a remark and context.
The employee is unsure whether the date was Monday or Tuesday.
The manager records immediate reporting through the proper route.
The person or area responsible provides record-handling instructions.
The supervisor adds an unsupported motive.
The account is posted for team voting.

Remove the name and assume all privacy concerns disappear.
responses: A learning output does not replace the complaint system.
This preserves both proper handling and the practice opportunity.
Other details may still identify the account and person.

lessons.transfer: Practice separating facts, uncertainty, and actions using a practice note only.

move.control: You can keep facts accurate and material within approved channels.
move.failure: A complaint becomes a learning artifact or an uncontrolled file.

lessons.title: Coordinate interim needs without punishing the reporter
lessons.summary: Identify a proposed work change that needs review for possible retaliatory effect.
lessons.objective: Identify a proposed work change that needs review for possible retaliatory effect.
objectives: Identify a proposed work change that needs review for possible retaliatory effect.
Distinguish support coordination from an assumed corrective finding.
Plan responsible-office review of a contested interim arrangement.
takeaways: Interim work needs require proper coordination.
Do not make reporting the reason for lost opportunity.
A temporary arrangement does not decide the allegation.
lessons.statement: An interim step should support the process without becoming punishment.

image.caption: Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

intro.heading: Coordinate interim needs without punishing the reporter
intro.body:
A report may raise immediate work-coordination needs while the authorized process continues. Those needs should be discussed with HR or other people or areas responsible. A manager should not independently decide corrective action outside assigned agency procedures or authority, punish or unnecessarily isolate the reporter, or assume that changing the reporter’s role is automatically the easiest way to reduce tension.

In the practice team, the manager proposes removing the employee from a visible project because the report has made meetings uncomfortable. That change may reduce opportunity because of reporting and needs appropriate review. A neutral-sounding label such as “protective move” does not establish that the arrangement is appropriate.

Preserve relevant work facts, obtain guidance, and explain what can properly be shared about any arrangement. A temporary measure does not prove or disprove the allegation. Professional work direction can continue, but its basis should remain relevant, documented through the proper process, and separate from resentment about the complaint.

inThisLesson: Identify a proposed work change that needs review for possible retaliatory effect.
Distinguish support coordination from an assumed corrective finding.
Plan responsible-office review of a contested interim arrangement.
What needs to happen?
lessons.keyStatement: An interim step should support the process without becoming punishment.

items.title: Work need
items.body: Identify the actual coordination issue: a meeting arrangement, contact concern, or coverage question. Present it to the person or area responsible for guidance. Do not assume the reporter should bear the change simply because removing that person is administratively easy or the person who reported the concern is seen as the source of tension.

items.title: Opportunity
items.body: Consider whether a proposed change reduces assignments, learning, visibility, or other opportunities after reporting. In the project case, the manager’s explanation explicitly connects exclusion to the complaint. Preserve that context and seek prompt review rather than accept a protective label as a complete justification.

items.title: No finding
items.body: An interim arrangement may be part of appropriate coordination without deciding the allegation. Explain operational responsibilities within information limits. Do not tell the team that the arrangement proves guilt, or that an unchanged arrangement means the concern was rejected. Findings belong to the authorized process.

tabs.label: Move the reporter
tabs.body: Moving the reporter can appear to resolve tension quickly, but may impose the cost of reporting on that person. It can reduce opportunity and discourage others. Obtain appropriate guidance about the actual need and proposed arrangement instead of using convenience as the rule.

tabs.label: Coordinated arrangement
tabs.body: A coordinated arrangement considers the work issue, effects, authority, and information limits. It may take more attention than a quick reassignment, but reduces the risk of an improvised punitive response. Keep its purpose separate from any final finding.

tabs.label: Business as excuse
tabs.body: Calling an action a business decision does not settle its basis. Legitimate work needs still require relevant evidence, and context matters after a report. Ask the person or area responsible to review a disputed change rather than assume the label makes it non-retaliatory.

check.question: What should happen before excluding the reporter from a visible project because of tension?
check.correct: Coordinate review of the proposed change, rationale, and possible retaliation concern with the person or area responsible.
wrong: Assume any protective label makes the change appropriate.
Treat exclusion as the normal price of reporting.
Announce that the temporary change proves the allegation.
check.feedbackCorrect: The proposed action and its effects need appropriate review; a label does not settle the question.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Protective language does not erase lost opportunity or the link to reporting. Exclusion is not the normal price of using the process, and an interim step is not a finding. Preserve the rationale and coordinate appropriate review before relying on the change.

items.text: Ask HR about an appropriate meeting arrangement.
Review coverage needs and the effects of a proposed change.
Remove learning work because the employee reported.
Warn a witness that participation will reduce standing.
A temporary assignment change proves guilt.
No temporary change proves the complaint was rejected.

options: Implement it because protection sounds positive.
Coordinate review of the work need, effect on opportunity, and possible retaliation concern.
Ask the team to choose which person loses the project.
responses: The label does not establish that the change is appropriate.
This checks the actual purpose and consequences through the person or area responsible.
A team vote is not the authorized process.

lessons.transfer: Describe a practice interim need, the proposed effect, and the question for HR without announcing a result.

move.control: You can identify the effects and seek appropriate guidance.
move.failure: A coordination step becomes punishment for reporting.

lessons.summary: Distinguish immediate reporting from completion of the entire response.
lessons.objective: Distinguish immediate reporting from completion of the entire response.
objectives: Distinguish immediate reporting from completion of the entire response.
Prepare an update within the leader’s authority and information limits.
Identify a general management practice to improve without disclosing a report.
takeaways: Immediate reporting begins coordination; it does not establish closure.
Follow agency guidance and appropriate update routes.
Improve response practices without using personal accounts as examples.
lessons.statement: Accountable follow-through keeps the concern in its proper process.

intro.heading: Follow the process and prevent a repeat of the response failure
intro.body:
Immediately reporting a concern is necessary, but not the same as completing every responsibility. Follow agency complaint and investigation procedures, respond to the person or area responsible’s requests within your role, and implement authorized actions appropriately. Avoid concluding that nothing remains because the initial email was sent.

In the practice team, the manager forwards the report but later ignores HR guidance about a contested assignment change. The reporting receipt documents one step, not complete follow-through. The leader should clarify the next responsibility and coordinate any unresolved issue rather than claim the process is finished.

Provide updates that you are authorized to give and direct detailed process questions to the person or area responsible. Improve general practices such as visible reporting information, timely routing, professional communication, and non-retaliatory assignment review. Keep real accounts and findings out of public learning stories. A course completion record demonstrates learning activity, not that an agency complaint was handled correctly or that all harassment risks are gone.

inThisLesson: Distinguish immediate reporting from completion of the entire response.
Prepare an update within the leader’s authority and information limits.
Identify a general management practice to improve without disclosing a report.
What should the leader check?
lessons.keyStatement: Accountable follow-through keeps the concern in its proper process.

items.title: Responsibility
items.body: Clarify the leader’s next role after the initial report. For example, the person or area responsible may need relevant work information or coordination of an authorized arrangement. Follow current agency instructions; do not create your own investigation or assume that sending the report ends all work.

items.title: Update
items.body: An appropriate update identifies the responsible contact or available next step without exposing restricted information or promising an outcome. If the employee asks for information beyond the leader’s role, consult the person or area responsible. Silence and unsupported reassurance both make the process harder to understand.

items.title: Practice improvement
items.body: Review the response practice using general or practice examples: did leaders know the reporting route, recognize the duty, and avoid proof gates? Improving that practice supports future response. It does not replace the actual investigation or justify using the complainant’s identifiable account in a team workshop.

tabs.label: Receipt as closure
tabs.body: A reporting receipt proves that one action occurred. It does not establish the response’s quality, final finding, or completion. Use it as a checkpoint and clarify any continuing responsibility through the person or area responsible.

tabs.label: Responsible follow-through
tabs.body: Responsible follow-through keeps actions tied to agency guidance and proper authority. It supports implementation and review without promising the outcome. The leader remains accountable for the work within the role while findings and release decisions stay with the proper process.

tabs.label: Universal success claim
tabs.body: A training or repaired routing practice can be encouraging but does not prove that all harassment and discrimination risks are eliminated. Report the specific improvement and remaining limits. Keep ongoing reporting routes and authorized response responsibilities visible.

check.question: After immediate reporting, what should the leader do?
check.correct: Follow current agency guidance, clarify continuing responsibilities, and provide only appropriate updates.
wrong: Treat the receipt as proof the entire matter is resolved.
Ignore responsible-office guidance about later work changes.
Use course completion as a finding of compliance.
check.feedbackCorrect: The report is a starting checkpoint; appropriate follow-through depends on the agency process and the leader’s actual role.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A receipt and course completion document activities, not a resolved complaint or complete compliance. Ignoring later guidance leaves a response gap. Clarify the remaining responsibility, coordinate appropriately, and keep updates proportional to what you are authorized to communicate.

lessons.next: Use the job aid to receive concerns seriously, report immediately, protect information and carry out any assigned duties within agency procedures and authorized responsibility. The course itself makes no finding or disciplinary decision.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: The manager has a reporting receipt but has not addressed later HR guidance and says the entire response is complete.

lessons.transfer: Identify the reporting checkpoint, continuing responsibility, appropriate update route, and one general practice improvement.

move.control: You can verify your continuing responsibilities and coordinate unresolved steps.
move.failure: An initial report is used to claim completion while required follow-through is missed.

jobAid.subtitle: Receive, report immediately, preserve facts appropriately, coordinate, and follow through.
remember: Do not wait for independent proof before the required reporting step.
Do not promise secrecy, a finding, or a disciplinary outcome.
Do not require confrontation or consultant approval before the proper route.

sections.heading: First response
items: Listen and acknowledge the concern without blame or a verdict.
Identify immediate-help needs and use established urgent procedures if needed.
Immediately report the allegation or incident to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer as required.

sections.heading: Information and next steps
items: Accurately preserve the account through the approved process.
Explain responsible contacts and applicable privacy limits.
Follow agency investigation procedures and responsible-office guidance.

sections.heading: Workplace follow-through
items: Coordinate any interim work arrangement through the proper authority.
Check for possible retaliation or discouraged participation.
Provide appropriate updates without exposing protected information or promising outcomes.
